anchor.quote: The basic unit of a bill is a clause (cl)
Bills often contain schedules. These are not units but are components of bills, Acts and some delegated legislation.
Units below clause level

Commonwealth bills refer to units below clause level using the smallest unit of text. This is a convention used by the Office of Parliamentary Counsel in legislative drafting. Some jurisdictions cite at clause level.

not_rules.note: Description of drafting conventions and jurisdictional differences.

anchor.quote: Whether to cite at clause level or below will depend on the context for your content. You can choose which method to follow.

Content that discusses the operation and effect of certain subclauses, paragraphs and subparagraphs will cite at the smallest unit level. A general discussion about the provisions of a bill will cite at clause level.
Follow in-house style. Otherwise, be guided by the type of content you’re writing, and its purpose and audience.
Shortened forms for units
The other units of bills mentioned above are also found in Acts.

You can use both the long and shortened forms of units for in-text citation and notes. To decide which to use, think about the type of content, its users and the amount of legal material cited in it. If the long form better helps people understand the text, use it.

not_rules.note: G-3: Permission granting choice between long and shortened forms.

anchor.quote: Explanatory material titles use roman type, title case
Explanatory material includes explanatory memoranda and explanatory statements.

An explanatory memorandum is a document tabled in parliament with a bill. It explains the objective of a proposed law and how it will operate. The Australian Government has provided explanatory memoranda with all government bills since 1982.

anchor.quote: An explanatory statement is a similar document that accompanies delegated legislation such as regulations and determinations.

rules.quote: Write the titles of bills in roman type, not italics.
rules.violation_condition: the title of a bill written in italics rather than roman type
rules.why: G-4: body states the direct prohibition against italics for bill titles.

covers.quote: The long title uses sentence case.

examples.note: Short title in title case without comma before year

parts.quote: A Bill for an Act to provide a legislative response to all people seeking asylum in Australia, and for related purposes

rules.quote: In general, use the short title. Use title case (maximal capitalisation). There is no comma between the title and year.
rules.violation_condition: a bill title that uses sentence case rather than title case, or that includes a comma between the title and the year
when: When using the short title of a bill (the default)
Exception: long titles use sentence case
rules.why: G-2: covers formatting of bill titles (title case and comma omission for short title, sentence case for long title).

covers.quote: If you are writing about 2 or more bills, use the lower case: ‘the bills’, ‘these bills’.
If you write about a bill or bills generally, use the lower case: ‘a bill’, ‘some bills’.
For bills, people are unlikely to find the lower case forms confusing. If there’s any chance the text is unclear to readers, use a capital ‘B’.

examples.note: Lower case 'bills' for multiple bills; capital 'Bill' in specific bill titles

parts.quote: The government drafted a legislative package that includes 3 bills:
the Human Rights Legislation Amendment (Freedom of Religion) Bill 2019.

rules.quote: Always use an initial capital for the word ‘Bill’ when you write about a specific bill: ‘the Bill’, ‘this Bill’.
rules.violation_condition: the word 'bill' written with a lower-case initial 'b' when referring to a specific bill
when: Applies when referring to a specific bill (e.g. 'the Bill', 'this Bill')
Does not apply when writing about 2 or more bills ('the bills') or bills generally ('a bill', 'some bills')
rules.why: G-2: capitalisation rules for the word 'bill' depending on whether reference is specific or general/plural.

examples.note: Capitalised because it begins a sentence

parts.quote: Clause 12 vests Commonwealth powers in the Minister …

rules.quote: Use lower case for these units of a bill unless they begin a sentence.
rules.violation_condition: initial capitalisation on unit names 'clause', 'subclause', 'paragraph' or 'subparagraph' when not beginning a sentence
when: Applies to units: clauses, subclauses, paragraphs, subparagraphs
Does not apply when the word begins a sentence
rules.why: Specific rule governing case of bill units below part level.

rules.quote: Always use an initial capital for these units, for example ‘Part 1’.
rules.violation_condition: the words 'part', 'division' or 'subdivision' written with a lower-case initial letter when citing or naming a specific unit
when: Applies to parts, divisions and subdivisions in bills
rules.why: Direct requirement for initial capitalisation of higher-level bill groupings (parts, divisions, subdivisions).

covers.quote: The shortened forms of ‘subclause’ and ‘subclauses’ are ‘subcl’ and ‘subcls’.

rules.quote: The shortened forms of ‘clause’ and ‘clauses’ are ‘cl’ and ‘cls’. Write them in lower case and without a full stop.
rules.violation_condition: abbreviations for clause/clauses or subclause/subclauses written in upper/title case, with a full stop, or using forms other than cl/cls/subcl/subcls
rules.why: G-2: rules for shortened forms of clause units consolidated into one rule.

examples.note: Explanatory Statement in title case and roman type

parts.quote: The Parliamentary Precinct Regulations 2011 allow the law governing the Parliamentary precinct to be applied to another location if Parliament House is unavailable due to a major event such as ‘an earthquake’ or ‘terrorist attack’ (Explanatory Statement, Select Legislative Instrument 2011 No. 181).

rules.quote: Write titles in roman type. Use title case for the titles of explanatory material.
rules.violation_condition: a title of explanatory material (explanatory memorandum or explanatory statement) written in italics or sentence case
rules.why: Direct formatting instruction for titles of explanatory material.

parts.quote: Material that does not form part of an Act (extrinsic material) can be used in the interpretation of an Act. Extrinsic material includes explanatory memorandums (EMs). The Legislation Register attaches an EM to each bill that is introduced.

rules.quote: Don’t use capitals for ‘explanatory memoranda’ and ‘explanatory statements’ when writing about explanatory material in the general sense.
rules.violation_condition: the terms 'explanatory memoranda', 'explanatory memorandums', or 'explanatory statements' capitalised when used in a general sense
when: When referring to explanatory material generally, not as part of a formal document title
rules.why: Prohibition against capitalising generic mentions of explanatory material.

covers.quote: For content that mentions explanatory material often, use these shortened forms:

examples.note: EMs defined in parentheses at first mention, then EM used alone

parts.quote: Material that does not form part of an Act (extrinsic material) can be used in the interpretation of an Act. Extrinsic material includes explanatory memorandums (EMs). The Legislation Register attaches an EM to each bill that is introduced.

rules.quote: Write them in parentheses at first mention and use the shortened form after that.
rules.violation_condition: using EM, EMs, or ES without introducing them in parentheses at first mention, or using full forms after introduction
when: For content that mentions explanatory material often and uses the shortened forms EM, EMs, or ES
rules.why: Standard acronym introduction rule applied specifically to EM / EMs / ES.
